# The Python package {#sec-python}

The package `biyos` calls the C library through `ctypes` and needs no compiled extension of its own, so one build serves every Python version from 3.10. A method takes the name of the C call it wraps, without the prefix: `BIYOS_addvar` is `model.addvar`, `BIYOS_setenvdblopt` and its kin are `env.setopt`, and the parameters keep their C names, such as `lb` and `ub`. Classes keep full names, except `Env` for the environment. Each follows the same rules as its C call, so the chapters before this one hold for Python as they do for C. This chapter covers what Python adds. @sec-pyapi lists every class and method.

## Environments and models {#sec-python-handles}

`Env()` creates an environment and `Model(env)` a model on it. Both are context managers, so a `with` block frees them when it ends, and both have a `close` method that does the same. Closing an environment closes every model made on it first. Using a closed environment or model raises `ValueError`, and closing one twice does nothing.

A model keeps its environment alive, so an environment the program no longer references stays allocated while one of its models is open. An environment or a model closed from inside one of its own calls, by a hook for instance, reads as closed at once and is freed when that call returns. A model closed by a hook during any other call reads as closed at once too, and is freed when the outermost call returns, where `BIYOS_freemdl` would fail ([Inside a hook](#sec-events-inside)).

## Blocks and views {#sec-python-blocks}

`addvar`, `addfun`, `addcon`, `addobj`, `addind`, `addsos`, `addcone` and `addccon` return a block: `Variables`, `Functions`, `Constraints`, `Objectives`, `Indicators`, `SOSs`, `Cones` or `Complements`. A block holds its model, the index of its first item and its count, so it costs the same whether it holds three items or three million. It supports `len`, iteration, indexing from either end and slicing with step 1:

```python
x = model.addvar(4)
len(x)        # 4
x[-1]         # the view of variable 3
x[1:3]        # a block of variables 1 and 2
```

Indexing a block gives a view, such as a `Variable`, which passes as its index wherever the model takes one: `int(x[2])` is 2. A whole block passes wherever the model takes a list of indices. A block or a `range` with step 1 goes to the `rg` form of the C call, two integers whatever its size, and any other sequence to the `sp` form; both give the same result, except that a range past the last item is refused even when it is empty. The model checks the family and the owner of each view and block, so passing a function where a variable is due, or a variable of another model, raises `ValueError` instead of naming the wrong item. `on` gives the block of the same indices in another model, such as a copy ([Copying in Python](#sec-copy-python)).

`delcon`, `delobj`, `delind`, `delsos`, `delcone` and `delccon` take a list, a range or a block, delete those items and return the map of @sec-model-deleting as a list. Once a call deletes an item, the indices of every block and view the model gave before may name other items, so the model refuses them with `ValueError`, whatever their family. A call that deletes nothing leaves them valid.

## Arrays {#sec-python-arrays}

A method that takes an array accepts any sequence of the right length: a list, a tuple, a block where indices are due. A sequence of the wrong length raises `ValueError`, an entry of the wrong type `TypeError`, and an integer too large for 32 bits `OverflowError`. A writable, contiguous buffer of doubles, such as an `array.array("d")`, passes to C without a copy where doubles are due; everything else is copied into a C array for the call. The annotations name sequences, so a type checker refuses a NumPy or a ctypes array, though both work at run time: a contiguous NumPy array of float64 is such a buffer and passes without a copy, while a ctypes array of doubles is copied. `None` stands for a null array and takes the default the C call gives it.

The readers return lists, in the order of the C call's arrays:

| Method | Returns |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| `getvar(idx)` | kinds, lower bounds, upper bounds |
| `getquadterm(idx)` | functions, first and second variables, coefficients |
| `getrlinterm(idx)` | functions, variables, coefficients |
| `getclinterm(idx)` | functions, variables, coefficients |
| `getexpr(idx)` | offsets, codes, arguments, values |
| `getcon(idx)` | functions, lower bounds, upper bounds |
| `getobj(idx)` | functions, senses, priorities, weights |
| `getind(idx)` | variables, values, functions, lower bounds, upper bounds |
| `getsos(idx)` | kinds, offsets, variables, weights |
| `getccon(idx)` | bounded functions, complementary functions, lower bounds, upper bounds |

`idx` lists the items to read, or is a block or a range of them, and defaults to every item, so `model.getvar()` reads them all. The readers of terms size their arrays themselves. `getrlinterm` reads the linear terms of functions and `getclinterm` those of variables, each term as its function, its variable and its coefficient, and `getnrlinterm` and `getnclinterm` count them. `getquadterm` reads the quadratic terms of functions in the same shape, with two variables, and `getnquadterm` counts them. `addlinterm(funidx, varidx, coef)` adds terms in that same shape, so `target.addlinterm(*source.getrlinterm())` copies the linear terms of one model into another with the same functions and variables. `addquadterm(funidx, varidx1, varidx2, coef)` does the same for quadratic terms, from `getquadterm`. `getsos` reads special ordered sets as `addsos` takes them, the members of each set from its offset, so `target.addsos(*source.getsos())` copies them into a model with the same variables, and `getnsosvar` counts the members. `getexpr` reads the expressions of functions in the postfix `addexpr` takes, its codes as `Operator` members, and `getnexpr` counts their entries and values, so `target.addexpr(*source.getexpr())` adds the expressions of one model to another, ready to attach ([Reading a model back](#sec-model-reading)).

A getter of an attribute takes the list of indices its setter takes and returns lists the same way: `model.getvarbnd(idx)` returns the lower and the upper bounds of the variables `idx` lists, and `model.getvarknd(idx)` their kinds. `getobjtol(idx)` returns the absolute and the relative tolerances of objectives, which `getobj` leaves out, as `addobj` does, and `getccontol(idx)` those of complements, None where a complement holds none. `getcst(idx)` returns the constants of functions, which `setcst` sets and `addcst` adds to.

## Constants {#sec-python-constants}

The C constants a program passes become `IntEnum` classes with the same values and full names: `VariableKind`, `Sense` and `SOSKind` for models, `EventKind` and `EventLevel` for events, `CheckLevel` for the values of `check_lvl` and `OptionSource` for where a model's option comes from, so `BIYOS_LVL_WARN` is `EventLevel.WARNING`. A reader returns them as members of their class, so `model.getvar()[0][0]` is `VariableKind.CONTINUOUS` rather than 1. Options are read and set by name ([Options in Python](#sec-options-python)).

## Failures {#sec-python-errors}

A failed C call raises `biyos.Error`, carrying the status as `code` and the message as its text. Mistakes the package catches before calling C raise Python's own exceptions, as [Errors in Python](#sec-errors-python) lists, and an exception raised in a hook is raised in the program once the call returns ([Events in Python](#sec-events-python)).
